title: Do ants find the shortest path? Both bridges open: 98% take the short one. Long bridge first: 0%.
description:
Do ants find the shortest path? One colony of 60 ants, two bridges from nest to food, the long bridge twice as long (a crossing takes 20 s on the short bridge, 40 s on the long one). Every ant leaves scent on the bridge it walks. At each choice an ant picks a bridge with probability proportional to (20 + scent)^2, Deneubourg's double-bridge rule; scent evaporates with a 600 s half-life. Both panels use the same random draws (seed 0, one numpy RandomState stream per ant). Top: both bridges open from the start. Bottom: only the long bridge for the first eight minutes, then the short bridge opens. Ten colony minutes play in 40 s.

Measured at seed 0:
- top, share of trips on the short bridge by minute: 64, 78, 84, 88, 93, 96, 97, 97, 99 and 98 percent; first minute at 80 percent or more: minute 3; over ten minutes 1,332 short trips against 138 long (90.6%); scent at minute 10: 995 on the short bridge, 85 on the long one
- bottom: 0 short trips in every minute, before and after the short bridge opens; over ten minutes 0 short trips against 830 long; scent at minute 10: 0 on the short bridge, 607 on the long one
- at minute 10: 98.0 percent on top, 0.0 percent below
- checks at seeds 1, 2 and 3: top 97.4, 96.7 and 98.7 percent; bottom 0.0 percent each time

Why: ants on the short bridge return sooner, so its scent builds faster and recruits more ants. But that feedback amplifies whichever bridge already carries scent, so a colony that found the long bridge first stays locked on it, as in the 1989 double-bridge experiments of Goss, Aron, Deneubourg and Pasteels with Argentine ants.

The numbers in the narration are the printed outputs of this exact run.

Made end to end by an AI agent: simulation, footage, voice, music, and edit.
